title: To Decide is to Cut
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. uses a colleague's story -- Tanya Ramm's account of a genuinely restful Labor Day weekend spent working only a few deliberately chosen hours -- to argue that the core skill of teacher time management isn't scheduling but deciding. He traces how Tanya had, over the previous year, stepped down from several extra commitments (NHS sponsor, PLC leader, MTSS committee) that she had taken on to be seen as a dedicated faculty member, and how shedding them left her lighter, more present, and by her own account a better teacher, not a worse one. Stuart builds from her story to a definition: to decide is literally to cut off, to say "this, not that," and argues teachers instinctively resist the "not that" half of any decision, trying instead to have it all. He reframes human finitude not as a limitation to fight but as "a feature," the very condition that makes a meaningful life possible, and connects the idea to Matthew Kelly's argument that the goal isn't work-life balance but harmony. The piece closes by naming deciding as the discipline the reader should practice getting better at this school year.
points: Tanya Ramm's story reframes rest not as time off but as time spent on purpose -- she worked fewer hours over the holiday weekend by design and reported it as her best weekend, not despite the work but because of how deliberately it was chosen.

Stepping down from extra commitments taken on to be seen as a "dedicated faculty member" (NHS sponsor, PLC leader, MTSS committee) is shown producing a better teacher, directly countering the assumption that more committee involvement signals more professional value.

The core definition -- "to decide is to cut off; to say, 'This, not that'" -- names the actual difficulty in decision-making as tolerating the loss of the rejected option, not choosing the accepted one.

Finitude is reframed from a limitation to be fought into "a feature" of being human, the very condition that makes a meaningful, chosen life possible, drawing on Matthew Kelly's harmony-over-balance argument.
quotes: What my colleague illustrated for me is the reality that teacher time management isn't as simple as working certain hours or certain days. It's instead about living on purpose — doing X because we've decided to do X, doing Y because we've decided to do Y, because these things align with our values and the lives we want to look back upon when we're older.
But as her non-renewed commitments accumulated behind her, Tanya felt lighter and lighter. The pressure she had felt — to be seen as a certain kind of faculty member — diminished.
To decide is to cut off; to say, "This, not that." It's the "not that" part that we tend to have a hard time with.

And here's the good news: finitude isn't a bug of being a human — it's a feature. In our finitude, we find the fixings for a life of meaning. But in ignoring our finitude, we end up frazzled, harried, burnt out, grumpy.
When we try having it all, doing it all, being it all, we end up shadows.
I love one of Kelly's central arguments in the book: that our aim shouldn't be a balance between work and life but rather a harmony.
